periods.analysis: Harborview’s childhood immunization rate is 96.8%, meeting the >=95% target and starting this eight-quarter view in green. With no prior quarter in this series, this is our baseline, and it shows that prevention is reaching most children before school and childcare exposure increases. The strongest contribution came from the August back-to-school clinics at Bayside Library, North Pier Elementary, and the Mariner Transit Center, where Public Health nurses reconciled state registry gaps before administering vaccines. This is a healthy population result, but it depends on routine follow-up, not one-time events.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the back-to-school clinic model in place and pre-booking the same three high-yield sites for 2025. Extend the Harborview Immunization Registry clean-up to pediatric practices on the Route 7 and Route 14 corridors, with weekly missing-dose lists sent to clinics each Friday. Maintain same-week nurse call-backs for families of children flagged as overdue for MMR, DTaP, or polio series completion.

periods.analysis: The rate is 96.0%, down 0.8 percentage points from 96.8% in 2024-Q3, but still green against the >=95% target. This small decline is consistent with the post-school-entry period, when the easiest catch-up opportunities have already been used and younger cohorts age into new dose requirements. Clinic staff noted more registry-lag cases among families changing providers between Harborview Pediatrics, Seacliff Family Medicine, and the county network, rather than a broad drop in vaccine acceptance. From a population-health standpoint, the system is still preventing outbreaks, but the margin above target narrowed.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by continuing monthly registry reconciliation with Harborview Pediatrics, Seacliff Family Medicine, and school nurses through the winter respiratory season. Add a specific watch-list for children turning 15 and 18 months old, since those cohorts are most likely to appear newly overdue after aging into the next dose window. Keep Saturday vaccine appointments at the South Harbor Clinic twice per month to reduce access-related delays for working families.

periods.analysis: Harborview improved to 96.5%, up 0.5 percentage points from 96.0% in 2024-Q4, keeping the measure green. The rebound suggests the winter registry work and Saturday access restored some of the Q4 slippage. Public Health’s nurse navigators closed gaps in the 15-month cohort by pairing reminder calls with appointments at South Harbor Clinic and the Cedar Point mobile van. This is the right pattern: identify children before they become long-term overdue and bring the dose to the family when transportation or scheduling is the barrier.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the gain by keeping the 15- and 18-month cohort report active and reviewing it at the first care-coordination huddle of each month. Extend Cedar Point mobile van hours by one evening during weeks when more than 40 children appear on the overdue list. Ask school district enrollment staff to continue flagging incomplete records within 48 hours so Public Health can resolve documentation before it becomes a true missed immunization.

periods.analysis: The rate rose to 97.6%, up 1.1 percentage points from 96.5% in 2025-Q1, the strongest performance so far in this sequence. This green result reflects early prevention work before summer travel and camp enrollment, especially the May “Ready for Summer” clinics at Bayfront Community Center and Harborview YMCA. The largest practical improvement came from same-day registry lookup and vaccine administration, which reduced the number of families asked to return for a second visit. At 97.6%, Harborview has a stronger buffer against normal seasonal movement while maintaining high community protection.
periods.recommendations: Sustain this level by making the “Ready for Summer” clinics an annual standing operation with dates published before spring break. Extend same-day registry lookup to all city-supported clinics by assigning one medical assistant per site as the registry lead. Preserve the high-performing Bayfront and YMCA locations, and add one smaller pop-up at East Dune Apartments if the overdue list shows more than 25 children in that census tract.

periods.analysis: The rate is 95.6%, down 2.0 percentage points from 97.6% in 2025-Q2, but it remains green and above the >=95% target. The decline is meaningful, not alarming: the denominator expanded with new kindergarten and childcare entries, including families arriving during Harborview’s summer move-in period. Public Health and school nurses found that many apparent misses were incomplete records from out-of-county providers, particularly around Harborview Heights Elementary and the new Shoreline Early Learning Center. The prevention system is still working, but the buffer is thinner and we should treat the fall enrollment transition as the watch point.
periods.recommendations: Sustain green status by repeating the back-to-school clinics, but add a dedicated records-resolution desk staffed by a registry specialist at Harborview Heights and Shoreline Early Learning Center. Extend text reminders in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Arabic to all families with provisional school enrollment status. Review the new-entrant list every Tuesday in September and route unresolved children to either their medical home or the Cedar Point mobile van within seven days.

periods.analysis: Harborview is at 95.4%, down 0.2 percentage points from 95.6% in 2025-Q3, still green but close enough to the target to keep our attention. The small decrease shows that the Q3 enrollment issue did not accelerate, which is reassuring, but it also did not fully reverse before year-end. Staff reported persistent documentation gaps among children who moved from regional clinics not connected cleanly to the state immunization registry. Clinically, this remains a strong prevention result; operationally, the remaining work is less about broad outreach and more about precise case closure.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by continuing case-by-case registry closure for provisional school records through January rather than ending the effort at winter break. Assign a Public Health nurse and one data technician to a weekly “last 100 charts” review focused on children missing only documentation or one final dose. Extend evening appointments at South Harbor Clinic through December for families contacted during the review.

periods.analysis: The rate improved to 95.9%, up 0.5 percentage points from 95.4% in 2025-Q4, keeping Harborview green and restoring some margin above the target. The “last 100 charts” work appears to have converted documentation gaps and single-dose misses into completed records. Pediatric partners also reported better uptake after the January well-child reminder campaign, especially for children approaching preschool entry. This is a good example of population health in practice: small, disciplined actions that prevent larger risks later.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the improvement by making the “last 100 charts” method a quarterly standard work item, not a special clean-up. Extend the January well-child reminder campaign to include automated portal messages from participating pediatric practices, with Public Health supplying the overdue-dose language. Track children approaching preschool entry as a named cohort and review completion rates before spring clinic scheduling is finalized.

periods.analysis: Harborview returned to 97.6%, up 1.7 percentage points from 95.9% in 2026-Q1, matching the high point reached in 2025-Q2 and remaining clearly green. The increase followed the combined preschool-entry cohort review, spring mobile clinics, and provider portal reminders, which together reduced both missed visits and missed documentation. The Bayfront Community Center, Harborview YMCA, and Cedar Point mobile van again produced strong turnout before summer travel began. The two-year arc shows a stable, high-performing immunization system with predictable seasonal dips that can be managed through targeted access and registry discipline.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 97.6% result by locking in the spring clinic calendar, mobile van staffing, and provider portal reminder schedule as the standard Q2 immunization package. Extend the approach to a year-round prevention dashboard that flags children 60 days before they become overdue, rather than after they miss a dose window. Keep special focus on school-entry and preschool-entry cohorts, because those transitions have been the clearest drivers of quarter-to-quarter movement.

periods.analysis: The carried-forward 97.6% is the June immunization result, 2.6 percentage points above target; it is not a newly observed September rate. The spring clinic and provider-portal work supports the favorable position, while back-to-school clinic completion provides an outreach update rather than a replacement for registry data.
periods.recommendations: Validate the September immunization rate against the provider registry and school-entry records before describing a Q3 change. Keep the mobile clinic and reminder schedule in place for children still due for doses.
